items.text: I usually feel comfortable with who I am, regardless of how things have gone recently.
When I do something well, I do not need other people to confirm it before I believe it myself.
My confidence in myself changes a lot depending on what other people say about me.
When something goes wrong, I can usually separate the event from my sense of who I am.
When I receive criticism, I sometimes question whether I deserve to be where I am.
When a situation starts going badly, I slow down and think before reacting.
After a setback, I usually focus on what I can do next rather than staying stuck in the problem.
Under pressure, I find it harder to notice what other people need from me.
During difficult conversations, I usually stay calm in how I speak and behave.
When something goes wrong, I often carry it with me for the rest of the day.
When I think a group is heading towards a poor decision, I usually say so before the decision is made.
When I make a commitment, I explain clearly what I will do and when I will do it.
I often avoid disagreeing with people whose opinion of me matters.
When something I am responsible for goes wrong, I tell the people affected before they discover it themselves.
I sometimes soften difficult messages so much that the main point becomes unclear.
When I discover I was wrong about something, I can usually admit it openly.
In the last six months, I have asked someone for honest feedback that might be uncomfortable to hear.
When something I am doing is not working, I tend to keep trying the same approach rather than change it.
In the last three months, I have deliberately done something difficult or unfamiliar.
When I talk about my weaknesses, I usually describe them as fixed rather than changeable.
When an interaction goes badly, I can usually recognise my part in it.
Before an important conversation, I usually notice the state I am in and think about how I want to show up.
Feedback from other people sometimes surprises me because it does not match how I see myself.
I usually notice changes in my energy, mood or focus before they affect other people.
I rarely discover that other people experienced me differently from how I intended.
When someone is telling me something difficult, I usually let them finish before responding.
I can often tell when someone is worried about something they have not said directly.
I often prepare my response before the other person has finished speaking.
Before offering solutions, I usually check what the other person wants from the conversation.
After a difficult conversation, I sometimes struggle to understand what mattered most to the other person.
In social or professional situations, I usually acknowledge the people around me.
When I meet someone again, I can often remember something specific about them.
The attention I give people sometimes depends on how useful they are to me.
I sometimes follow up with people after meaningful conversations, even when there is no task involved.
I naturally give more warmth and attention to important people than to less important people.
My follow-up questions are usually based on what the other person has just said.
When I meet someone new, I usually try to learn something about them beyond their job title.
In conversation, I sometimes relate things back to myself before fully hearing the other person.
When discussing opinions, I usually make space for other points of view.
I behave very differently in formal situations compared with informal ones.
When someone disagrees with me in front of others, I usually stay steady in how I respond.
When shared work is praised, I make sure other people receive credit as well.
When I do not know something, I sometimes try to hide it rather than admit it.
When I am the most senior or experienced person in a group, I usually encourage others to speak first.
I am more careful about how I behave with people I want to impress than with everyone else.
I give the same quality of attention to junior people as I do to senior people.
I behave differently when I know I am being judged or evaluated.
People who know me in different parts of my life would probably describe me in similar ways.
When I am tired or distracted, the quality of my attention towards other people drops noticeably.
I invest time and attention in people even when they have nothing obvious to offer me.

authenticityBands.label: Consistently available
authenticityBands.description: Behaviour is not conditional on status, usefulness, or familiarity. The same principle shows up across audiences, with appropriate surface adaptation.

authenticityBands.label: Broadly consistent
authenticityBands.description: Behaviour is reliable in most settings, with one or two specific contexts that narrow it.

authenticityBands.label: Selectively deployed
authenticityBands.description: Skills are real but unevenly distributed. Inner ring gets the full version. Peripheral contacts get less.

authenticityBands.label: Significantly instrumental
authenticityBands.description: Behaviour is at its strongest when it serves a purpose. The transactional logic is visible to others.

incidentally_invisible.label: The Incidentally Invisible
incidentally_invisible.tagline: Talented but overlooked. Ability is not the gap. Visibility is.

unknowingly_influential.label: The Unknowingly Influential
unknowingly_influential.tagline: Connects naturally. Undersells consistently. Influence outruns reputation.

occasionally_overconfident.label: The Occasionally Overconfident
occasionally_overconfident.tagline: Commands attention. Loses the room when warmth or restraint is the test.

courteously_charismatic.label: The Courteously Charismatic
courteously_charismatic.tagline: Competent and connected. The work is consistency. Closing the gap between best and average.
